candidates.text: We also teach our models how to apply these principles by incorporating user signals like thumbs-up / thumbs-down feedback on ChatGPT responses.
candidates.speaker_or_outlet: OpenAI, blog post 'Sycophancy in GPT‑4o: What happened and what we’re doing about it'
candidates.verified_how: Page opened via TinyFish fetch; quote copied verbatim from the page text. The page uses a non-breaking hyphen in 'GPT‑4o' and a curly apostrophe in 'we’re'. Trim with ellipses if needed, e.g. '…incorporating user signals like thumbs-up / thumbs-down feedback on ChatGPT responses.'

The same post says the update 'skewed towards responses that were overly supportive but disingenuous' because it 'focused too much on short-term feedback'. Best shown right after the news headlines as the 'mechanism' beat.

candidates.text: OpenAI explains why ChatGPT became too sycophantic
candidates.verified_how: Page opened via WebFetch and TinyFish fetch. Page title is 'OpenAI explains why ChatGPT became too sycophantic | TechCrunch'; byline Kyle Wiggers. Body describes users noticing ChatGPT 'applauding all sorts of problematic, dangerous decisions and ideas', which 'quickly became a meme'.
candidates.why_it_fits: 47 characters and phone-friendly (about 2 s). It names the flattery directly, for the 'who likes me' beat. Verified alternate: NBC News, 'OpenAI rolled back a ChatGPT update that made the bot excessively flattering', Angela Yang, 2025-04-30 (https://www.nbcnews.com/tech/tech-news/openai-rolls-back-chatgpt-after-bot-sycophancy-rcna203782; page opened via TinyFish fetch and matches).

Science DOI 10.1126/science.aec8352 was bot-blocked, so its title and date come from a search index. NPR (Ari Daniel, 2026-04-23, page opened) confirms the paper appeared in Science.

Use the abstract's 50% figure only; NPR's coverage gives 51% for one subset and 47% overall, so do not mix them.
